title: How do you manage secrets and connection strings in .NET applications?
description: user-secrets for development, Key Vault and managed identities for production, rotation and log hygiene.

data.text: **Question:** How do you manage secrets and connection strings in .NET applications?

Secrets never live in source control. In development, use **dotnet user-secrets** (a JSON file outside the repo, loaded via `AddUserSecrets`). In production, inject them from the platform — environment variables, Azure Key Vault / AWS Secrets Manager — and prefer **managed identity** so there is no secret to store at all: the workload authenticates with its own identity. The configuration system reads them through `IConfiguration` exactly like any other setting, so swapping the source needs no code change.

**Layered approach:**
- **Development:** `dotnet user-secrets` keeps values in `%APPDATA%\microsoft\UserSecrets\<id>` (or `~/.microsoft/usersecrets`), wired up with `builder.Configuration.AddUserSecrets(...)` — marked with `[assembly: UserSecretsId]` in Development only
- **Non-production servers:** environment variables (`ConnectionStrings__OrdersDb`) — the double underscore nests keys; twelve-factor style
- **Production:** cloud secret store (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager) mounted into configuration; rotate on a schedule and on breach
- **Best case — no secret at all:** managed identity / workload identity: the app authenticates to the database or service with its platform identity (e.g. Azure AD auth to SQL), so nothing sensitive is stored anywhere
- Access is logged and auditable at the vault; roles are granted per secret

data.title: Development secrets vs production vault

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing user-secrets is a **development** tool, not a production one
- The configuration-provider pattern: code reads IConfiguration, sources change per environment
- Production thinking: vault + rotation + audit + least privilege
- Awareness that managed identities remove whole categories of risk

items: Committing appsettings.Production.json with real values or a `.env` file with credentials
Printing the full configuration tree at startup — it lands in logs and dashboards
Hard-coding secrets in code or build pipelines instead of injecting them at runtime
Never rotating keys, or rotating without zero-downtime overlap
Using one shared secret for every environment and service — no blast-radius control
Assuming user-secrets works the same on the production server
How would you rotate a database password without restarting every service?
What is the precedence order of configuration providers in a default ASP.NET Core app?
How does an app authenticate to Key Vault — what does DefaultAzureCredential try, in order?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: user-secrets in development, environment variables/vault in production
Code always reads IConfiguration — the source is a deployment concern
Managed identity means no stored credential at all
Rotate secrets, audit access, and keep them out of logs
data.takeaway: Treat secrets as runtime configuration from a vault — never as files in the repository — and prefer platform identities over stored credentials.
